activities.anchor: Try it on an idiom and watch it fail
activities.caption: two theories of the job — drag the divider
activities.name: trUnitCompare

config.prompt: The same sentence, two philosophies of translating it — drag the divider:

before.label: word-for-word
before.text: pets falling from the sky — nonsense to a German or Japanese reader; accurate about the words, false about the message

after.label: message-for-message
after.text: 'it is raining very hard', expressed the way a native speaker naturally would — the idea, re-coded

config.why: The unit of work is the message, not the word.

activities.anchor: its own techniques, and its own professional standards
activities.caption: two thousand years of theory — pair each voice with its claim
activities.name: trTheorMatch

config.prompt: Match each theorist to their position:

pairs.right: not word for word, but sense for sense
the same position — scripture excepted, where the words themselves are mysteries
languages differ in what they must convey, not what they may convey
translate for the purpose of the target text — the brief, not the source, sets the goal

config.why: Jakobson's line explains why full equivalence is impossible in principle and translation always remains possible: the message can be recoded.

activities.caption: the layers of meaning — file each example
activities.name: trLayerSort

config.prompt: Translation fails at whichever layer it ignores — file each by its layer:

items.label: 'the door is closed' — the dictionary proposition
contract language versus text messages — the formality level
'can you pass the salt?' — a request, not a question about ability

config.why: Japanese encodes social hierarchy in verb endings and English does not — identical denotations can carry different social meanings, and the translator decides which layers matter for this text.

activities.anchor: classic distinction still organises the craft
activities.caption: you set the equivalence — three texts, three positions
activities.name: trEquivBranch

config.root: Three texts land on your desk. Set each position on the formal–dynamic spectrum.

start.text: Text one: a contract clause whose enforceable force lives in its wording.

choices.label: Formal — keep the structure visible
choices.feedback: Same sentence shapes, same ambiguities — the choice for anything whose form is its meaning.

choices.label: Dynamic — reproduce the reader's experience
choices.feedback: The enforceable force lived in the structure; loosening it changed the meaning.

n1.text: Position held. Text two: scripture studied for its words as mysteries.

choices.label: Formal — even the ambiguities
choices.feedback: Form carries ritual weight; the words themselves are the object of study.

choices.label: Dynamic — smooth it for modern readers
choices.feedback: A study text wants the source's shape; smoothing erases what is being studied.

n2.text: Position held. Text three: 'gird up your loins', for a modern audience.

choices.label: Dynamic — 'prepare yourself for action'
choices.feedback: Nida's own example: the original's readers received an exhortation to readiness, not a clothing instruction.

choices.label: Formal — 'gird up your loins'
choices.feedback: The modern reader receives a clothing instruction where the original gave an exhortation.

n3.text: Three positions, all chosen by function — most real texts live between the poles, sentence by sentence.

dyn1.text: Mispositioned — in legal documents the form is the meaning.

dyn2.text: Mispositioned — scripture study keeps the structure visible, even the same ambiguities.

dyn3.text: Mispositioned — the effect the original carried was readiness, and the reader is the test.

config.why: Formal equivalence keeps the source's structure visible; dynamic equivalence reproduces the reader's experience — neither pole is 'the answer'.

activities.caption: true or false — the invisible-translation myth
activities.name: trInvisJudge

statements.s: A good translation is invisible and interchangeable with the original.
statements.why: Translators make interpretive choices — visible or invisible is itself a choice.

statements.s: Two excellent translations of the same poem can differ substantially.
statements.why: They are two readings of one text — both may reach the effect.

statements.s: Equivalence to the words is the professional standard.
statements.why: Equivalence to the effect is the standard.

activities.anchor: analysis step amateurs skip and machines cannot perform
activities.caption: fill the four questions of the analysis
activities.name: trAnalCloze

config.text: The classic questions of source-text analysis: what is this text %%0%% (informing, persuading, regulating, entertaining)? %%1%% is it for (specialists, consumers, regulators, children)? What is its %%2%% and tone (legalese, breezy marketing, clinical neutrality)? And what is its %%3%% — where will the translation appear, and what must it accomplish there?
config.hint: The commissioning client's translation brief states the last two institutionally.

activities.caption: clause vs slogan — drag the divider
activities.name: trTaskCompare

config.prompt: One morning, two jobs — drag the divider:

before.label: the liability clause
before.text: form is meaning — 'shall not be liable' and 'arising from' carry the enforceable force; reproduce it in the target legal system's idiom

after.label: the slogan
after.text: the meaning is rhythm, imperative warmth, brand association — rebuild them with new words, possibly a new joke; the words themselves are not the product

config.why: Only the analysis step tells you which job you are on — and in legal, technical and medical registers a wrong term is a factual error.

activities.caption: the spectrum, from gloss to adaptation
activities.name: trSpecOrder

config.prompt: Two millennia of contest resolved as a spectrum — order it, most literal first:
config.why: Positions are chosen per text and per sentence — the translator's skill is knowing which position a given sentence demands, and being able to defend the choice.
